title: US Intelligence Ties a Businesswoman Close to Jensen Huang to Beijing, and the Megaspeed Channel Comes Back Into Focus
subhead: A New York Times report alleging a Chinese intelligence asset inside Nvidia's largest Southeast Asian customer lands the same week Nvidia is lobbying Washington to loosen the AI chip rules, giving export-control hardliners their strongest argument in months.

sections.heading: The Megaspeed Case Turns From Compliance Problem to Counterintelligence Problem
sections.body:
US intelligence agencies have concluded that a Chinese businesswoman who built a close relationship with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was working on Beijing's behalf, according to a New York Times report published this week and confirmed in its broad particulars by Bloomberg and CNBC reporting. The woman was a former executive at Megaspeed International, the Singapore-based cloud operator that grew from a small unit of a Chinese gaming company into Nvidia's largest customer in Southeast Asia.

Huang's response, given Thursday to Bloomberg, was that Nvidia's dealings with Megaspeed were 'normal and not unusual' and that the company had 'studied all their deployments of our GPUs and counted every one.' In separate statements, Nvidia called Megaspeed a typical regional cloud customer and said earlier allegations that the firm funneled chips to China were 'thoroughly investigated and debunked last year.' Megaspeed did not respond to requests for comment; the Justice Department and FBI declined to comment.

The distinction matters. Megaspeed was already under scrutiny last year over the possible diversion of H100 and H200 processors through Singapore and Malaysia, and Singapore charged three men in 2025 in a case involving servers that may have carried Nvidia chips bound for China. That was a compliance question a company could answer with an audit. An intelligence asset inside a major customer is a different category — one where the chipmaker is a target, not a defendant. Huang's 'counted every one' answers the first and sidesteps the second.
sections.whyItMatters: Nvidia has spent 2026 arguing in Washington that export controls should be eased so it can sell to China, citing substantial inventory write-offs after Beijing blocked imports of American AI chips. A counterintelligence case running through its own Southeast Asian channel strengthens the hand of officials who want the rules tightened instead — and it will be weighed on what investigators find, not on deployment records.

sections.heading: A $1 Trillion Chip Rout Gives the Politics a Financial Backdrop
sections.body:
The Nvidia story landed into the worst week for semiconductors in years. Intel fell 29 to 30 percent on Friday to close near $65.76, erasing more than $146 billion in market value — its worst single-day decline in over 50 years, according to Decrypt and Reuters. Semiconductor stocks collectively lost roughly $1 trillion in market value on the day, and the Nasdaq dropped nearly 3 percent.

The cause was a fourth-quarter guide, not a bad quarter. Intel's third-quarter revenue rose 21 percent year on year to $16.5 billion, and its Data Center and AI division grew 78 percent to $7.3 billion with $3 billion in operating profit. But Intel forecast Q4 revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion against an analyst consensus of $17.07 billion, and guided non-GAAP gross margin down to 38 percent from 44.1 percent. CFO Dave Zinsner blamed weak PC demand, manufacturing constraints on server processors and an accident at a factory in Israel, and said Intel probably will not generate positive free cash flow next year.
sections.whyItMatters: The selloff was not a verdict on AI demand — it was a verdict on who can physically deliver it. Intel has the orders and cannot make the chips, while its traditional PC business contracts through 2027 and its fab expansion consumes cash. That is the gap the US CHIPS-era industrial policy was supposed to close, and Friday's move shows investors now pricing the difficulty of closing it.

sections.heading: The FCC Moves on Three Fronts at Once Against Chinese Telecoms
sections.body:
The FCC said on Thursday it will vote on November 19 on a proposal barring China Mobile, China Telecom, China Unicom and other IP-enabled service providers from direct access to US phone numbers and IP-enabled networks, Reuters reported. The stated rationale is twofold: curbing illegal robocalls routed through vulnerable channels, and national security — a reference to the Salt Typhoon intrusions into US broadband and telecom infrastructure.

In the same session the commission voted to bar all Chinese laboratories from testing electronic devices — smartphones, cameras, computers — for the US market, effective December 2028. FCC Chair Brendan Carr has said 82 percent of electronics were tested in China, which has no mutual-recognition agreement with the US, while fewer than 4 percent were tested in US labs. The agency also floated barring Chinese firms from connecting to US networks and operating US data centers.

Beijing pushed back sharply. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said China 'firmly opposes and deplores' the moves and would 'do what is necessary to firmly defend its legitimate and lawful rights and interests.' Writing in the Global Times, researcher Zhang Xiaorong argued the lab ban presumes risk 'solely on the basis of national origin' without evidence of violations, and trade researcher Zhou Mi warned of adjustment costs for firms that depend on Chinese testing capacity. Testing firm Element has cautioned that relocating testing will lengthen lead times and raise costs because labs sit next to factories.
sections.whyItMatters: This pushes the US-China tech split from equipment and chips into certification and numbering — the plumbing that decides whether a device can legally be sold and whether a call can be completed. Unlike a fab subsidy, these measures take effect on a fixed date and force supply chains to re-route around a specific country rather than a specific company.

sections.heading: CrowdStrike: a Chinese Group Used Agentic AI Against 200-Plus Targets in Two Weeks
sections.body:
CrowdStrike attributed a campaign beginning October 17 to the China-linked group it tracks as Vapor Panda, which used a Go-based AI penetration-testing framework called ARTEX against more than 200 distinct organizations worldwide. Targets named in the Thursday analysis include the foreign ministries of two Latin American countries, a Central American government and an Asian one; a Middle East interior ministry; a European country's foreign ministry, presidency and prime minister's office along with its defense, justice, finance and intelligence entities; 19 US organizations in pharmaceuticals, semiconductors, defense, nuclear and finance; and telecom providers in the US, Belgium and the Philippines.

Post-exploitation was confirmed at nine organizations, where attackers deployed BLOODALCHEMY, a ShadowPad derivative, then moved to credential spraying and lateral movement. The framework ran on DeepSeek plus an unidentified subscription commercial LLM, with planner and worker agents coordinating under a human operator. In one intrusion, CrowdStrike measured planning agents consuming on the order of 1.4 billion input tokens.

The disclosure came alongside four previously undocumented China-linked clusters — Hollow Panda, Overcast Panda, Titan Panda and Veiled Panda. Overcast Panda is described as deploying its FlowCloud backdoor via direct physical access to devices of people traveling in China; Titan Panda exploited a hard-coded IIS machine key in Intapp Time Server to breach law firms.
sections.whyItMatters: The throughput is the story. Agentic tooling let a small team run parallel attack paths across web apps, cloud, containers, Active Directory and VPN infrastructure at a tempo manual operations cannot match. Defensive economics built around analyst headcount now face an attacker whose marginal target is cheap.

sections.heading: India Restores NavIC to Minimum Operating Strength With NVS-03
sections.body:
ISRO launched NVS-03 aboard GSLV-F18 at 11:51 pm Friday from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre, injecting the 2,250 kg satellite into a geosynchronous transfer orbit after an 18-minute flight. ISRO chief V. Narayanan said the launch restored India's independent position, navigation and timing services, bringing the NavIC constellation back to its minimum operational configuration of four satellites — NVS-01 plus three others.

The satellite carries an indigenous rubidium atomic clock and will transmit in the L1, L5 and S bands from a slot at 32.5 degrees east, covering India and a 1,500 km radius beyond its borders. ISRO cited a 56-day turnaround between GSLV missions, its shortest yet. The agency says NavIC is a core input to the 'one nation, one time' project, following the government's notification of the Legal Metrology (Indian Standard Time) Rules, 2026. Prime Minister Narendra Modi called the mission 'an important step in strengthening NavIC.'
sections.whyItMatters: India is the only country other than the US, Russia, China and the EU running a regional navigation system, and it has just spent a launch slot replacing capacity rather than adding it. Timing signals are what financial networks, power grids and telecoms synchronize to; a four-satellite constellation is a floor, not a margin.

sections.heading: Rare-Earth Prices Split Into Two Markets, and Lynas Signs Floors to Exploit It
sections.body:
Australia's Lynas Rare Earths, the only major producer of separated rare earths outside China, said Thursday it has secured minimum-price agreements covering more than half its production. Average selling prices jumped 88 percent to a record A$102.1 per kg in the quarter to September 30, lifting revenue 55 percent to A$310.1 million even as sales volumes fell 18 percent year on year. Interim CEO Pol Le Roux said 'there is a real strategy from OEMs to secure part of their supply from outside China.'

NdPr oxide output hit a quarterly record of 2,082 tonnes. The company also agreed this month to buy Meteoric Resources in an all-share deal valued at A$968 million, adding Brazil's Caldeira project, with mixed carbonate planned for shipment to Malaysia for separation. Lynas shares rose 4.2 percent Thursday, then fell 7.1 percent Friday.

Separately, Malaysia confirmed its ban on raw rare earth exports remains in force despite the October 2025 US-Malaysia critical minerals memorandum. Natural resources minister Arthur Joseph Kurup told Parliament in February that the agreement carries no exclusive supply obligations, and the reciprocal trade agreement itself never entered into force.
sections.whyItMatters: Two things are happening at once: a premium market outside China is forming, and governments are keeping raw material at home to capture downstream value. Lynas locking price floors turns the China discount into a hedgeable contract — but the December quarter brings a month-long Malaysian plant shutdown and a two-week Kalgoorlie outage, so the supply being contracted is not yet the supply being delivered.

sections.heading: Binance's $6.3 Billion Breach Is Attributed to North Korea, and Washington Is Still Deciding What It Thinks
sections.body:
Blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs attributed the $6.3 billion Binance breach to TraderTraitor, the North Korean unit blamed for last year's $1.5 billion Bybit heist, with 'high confidence.' Chainalysis and Elliptic also linked the theft to North Korea; Binance has not confirmed attribution. TRM says most of the funds were moved from Binance wallets across 10 blockchain networks in about 20 minutes, which would make it the largest crypto theft on record and plausibly the single largest heist of any kind.

Binance has set aside roughly $6.34 billion in company funds to cover losses, per Reuters, and says partners have frozen about $3 billion in affected assets. Withdrawals were expected to resume within 48 hours, and deposits had already reopened. President Trump said Friday his administration was looking into the incident and that the US does not yet know whether North Korea was responsible.
sections.whyItMatters: Sanctions regimes assume stolen crypto must be laundered and can be traced to a point of cash-out. A 20-minute, ten-chain extraction with $3 billion already frozen shows both sides of that race running simultaneously at scale. The dispute over attribution — three private firms on one side, an open White House position on the other — is itself a live test of who gets to speak authoritatively about state-linked financial crime.

bottomLine: Nvidia's export-control argument took its heaviest hit of the year on the counterintelligence front just as the chip sector absorbed a $1 trillion rout driven by Intel's inability to manufacture what it sells — two different symptoms of the same gap between demand for AI compute and the physical capacity to supply it. In parallel, Washington moved to sever Chinese carriers' access to US numbering and to end Chinese lab testing of US electronics, Beijing promised countermeasures, and CrowdStrike documented a Chinese group applying agentic AI to over 200 targets in two weeks. The through-line is that enforcement is getting more specific: named firms, named labs, named customers, dated votes. That precision raises the cost of each measure and makes the retaliation easier to target.
sources: New York Times (via HNGN, cybernews, Hindustan Times), Bloomberg, CNBC, Reuters, Decrypt, MarketWatch, Baltimore Sun, The News International, Global Times, CrowdStrike via The Hacker News, ETV Bharat, PTI, Xinhua, Mining.com, Startup Fortune, TRM Labs, Elliptic via Mashable, Chainalysis via Yahoo Finance
